bars:Cava — invented Penedès 1872.name: Cava
bars:Cava — invented Penedès 1872.teaser: Bottle-fermented on Penedès grapes, and the back label tells you exactly how long it sat on its lees
bars:Cava — invented Penedès 1872.story: Cava is made like champagne, second fermentation in the bottle, but from Catalan grapes: Macabeu for freshness, Xarel·lo for body and salt, Parellada for perfume. The 1872 first bottle belongs to Sant Sadurní d'Anoia, and so does about three-quarters of today's output. What matters at the table is time on the lees. The DO's ladder runs Cava de Guarda (9 months), Reserva (18), Gran Reserva (30) and Cava de Paraje Calificado, a single named plot with at least 36 months. Some of the best growers no longer say Cava at all: they bottle as Corpinnat, the Penedès breakaway brand.
bars:Cava — invented Penedès 1872.why: Pay a little more for a Reserva or Gran Reserva with a vintage on it; that is where cava stops being party fizz.
facts: Fine bubbles, green apple and almond on a young one; bread, toast and salt as the lees time grows
Green seal for Cava de Guarda, silver for Reserva, gold for Gran Reserva; Paraje Calificado names its plot; Corpinnat means the grower left the DO
Un cava brut nature reserva, or a Corpinnat by the glass; EUR 12–80 a bottle in shops (seen Jul 2026)

bars:Vermut — Yzaguirre Reus 1884.name: Vermut
bars:Vermut — Yzaguirre Reus 1884.teaser: Red vermut on ice with an orange slice and an olive, a siphon on the table, sometime between noon and two
bars:Vermut — Yzaguirre Reus 1884.story: Vermut is wine fortified and steeped with botanicals, wormwood above all, plus gentian, citrus peel and cinnamon: sweet first, bitter last, amber to mahogany, around 15 to 18 percent. Most of what Barcelona pours comes from Reus, south of the city, where the industry grew from the late 1800s (Yzaguirre, founded 1884, has its own card). Here it is poured from the tap or the bottle over ice, with a slice of orange and an olive on a stick, and lengthened with a squirt from the soda siphon. The plate beside it never changes: olives, crisps, anchovies, a tin of cockles or mussels.
bars:Vermut — Yzaguirre Reus 1884.why: Order the house vermut from the tap (de la casa, de grifo) and the cheapest tin on the list; that is the ritual.
facts: Red (negre) is sweet, herbal and bitter at the end; white (blanc) is drier and more floral
Vermut de Reus for the Tarragona houses; reserva on a bottle means it was rested in wood
Un vermut negre de la casa amb sifó, with olives and boquerons; EUR 3–7 a glass (seen Jul 2026). Bar Bodega Quimet, Morro Fi and Els Sortidors del Parlament have their own table cards

bars:Priorat — DOQ since 2000.name: Priorat
bars:Priorat — DOQ since 2000.teaser: Old Garnatxa and Carinyena rooted in black slate, from a region that went from forgotten to famous in a decade
bars:Priorat — DOQ since 2000.story: Priorat, about two hours south of the city, is one of only two Spanish wine regions with the top qualified rank: DOQ in Catalan, DOCa in Spanish, the other being Rioja. Its soil is llicorella, crumbling black slate flecked with mica, so poor that vines push roots metres down and give tiny yields. In 1989 five newcomers, René Barbier, Álvaro Palacios, Daphne Glorian, Carles Pastrana and Josep-Lluís Pérez, pooled their first vintages from steep terraces around Gratallops; the wines, sold under the names of their 'Clos', changed the region's fortunes. Expect power: dark fruit, warm stone, graphite, often 14.5 percent or more.
bars:Priorat — DOQ since 2000.why: For half the price, the Montsant DO that rings Priorat grows the same grapes on gentler ground.
facts: Inky Garnatxa and Carinyena: black cherry, liquorice, warm slate; big alcohol, firm tannin
DOQ Priorat; a Vi de Vila names its village (Gratallops, Porrera, Torroja), Vi de Finca a single estate
A Priorat with red meat at dinner, or a Montsant by the glass; EUR 35 to well over 1,000 a bottle (seen Jul 2026)

bars:Xarel·lo — Penedès still white.name: Xarel·lo
bars:Xarel·lo — Penedès still white.teaser: The backbone grape of cava, now bottled still: saline, firm and built to age
bars:Xarel·lo — Penedès still white.story: For a century Xarel·lo was the workhorse in the cava blend, valued for body and its resistance to oxidation. A generation of Penedès and Alella growers now bottles it on its own, still, from old vines, and it turns out to be one of the Mediterranean's most serious whites: lemon peel, fennel, a salty finish and enough structure to keep for years. In Alella, on the granite-sand soil called sauló just north of the city, it goes by Pansa Blanca. Names to look for include Alta Alella, Recaredo and Gramona, and Costador's natural bottlings from very old vines.
bars:Xarel·lo — Penedès still white.why: Order it with pa amb tomàquet, salt cod or prawns; it was made for exactly that.
facts: Pale gold, lemon, fennel and green almond, a saline finish
Xarel·lo or Pansa Blanca; DO Penedès, DO Alella or Classic Penedès
Un xarel·lo blanc, ideally from old vines (vinyes velles); EUR 14–35 a bottle (seen Jul 2026)

bars:Ratafia — the Catalan herbal.name: Ratafia
bars:Ratafia — the Catalan herbal.teaser: Green walnuts picked around Sant Joan, steeped in spirit with dozens of herbs, poured cold after coffee
bars:Ratafia — the Catalan herbal.story: Ratafia is the farmhouse liqueur of inland Catalonia. Around Sant Joan, at the end of June, the walnuts are picked while still green and soft-shelled, then cut and macerated in spirit with a blend of herbs and spices: mint, lemon verbena, thyme, cinnamon, clove and many more. The jar sits in the sun for about forty days; the walnuts turn the liquid deep brown and give it a bitter edge that the sugar rounds off. Every family and village has its recipe, Montseny and Santa Coloma de Farners above all. Since 2017 Ratafia Catalana has been a protected geographical indication.
bars:Ratafia — the Catalan herbal.why: End a long lunch with a small, cold glass of it; it does more than another coffee.
facts: Dark amber, walnut and herb bitterness, sweet and warming
Ratafia Catalana IGP, made anywhere in Catalonia; small makers often add their village
Una ratafia freda after coffee; EUR 18–35 a bottle (seen Jul 2026)

natural-wine:Bar Salvatge.name: Bar Salvatge
natural-wine:Bar Salvatge.teaser: A Gràcia wine bar with eight natural wines on tap and a hippo behind the bar on the logo
natural-wine:Bar Salvatge.story: Salvatge means wild, and the bar on Carrer de Verdi is given over to natural wine and its growers. Eight wines run from rotating taps, more by the bottle, and glasses start low enough to try several. The room is wood, communal tables and a neon sign; the food is deliberately simple, cheese and cured meat boards to carry the wine. The staff know the producers and will pour a taste before you commit. Verdi is the street of Gràcia's independent cinema and late bars, so it makes a natural end to an evening in the quarter.
natural-wine:Bar Salvatge.why: Ask what came on tap this week and let them pour you two small tastes side by side.
facts: Natural wine from eight rotating taps, with a cheese board
Glasses from about EUR 2 to 6 (Time Out, seen Oct 2026)

natural-wine:Bar Zim.name: Bar Zim
natural-wine:Bar Zim.teaser: Fifteen stools in a Gothic Quarter vault, wine by the glass and cheese from the shop next door
natural-wine:Bar Zim.story: Behind a heavy door on Carrer de la Dagueria, Bar Zim holds about fifteen stools inside old stone walls, and you will probably walk past it once before you find it. It is run by the team of the Formatgeria La Seu cheese shop next door (which has its own card), so the wine list, mostly Catalan and lesser-known Spanish bottles, is chosen to go with what comes off the cheese board, plus olives or jamón. The owner talks wine with real knowledge. It is cash only, cards and photographs are not welcome, and when the stools are full you wait.
natural-wine:Bar Zim.why: Put yourself in their hands: one glass, one cheese, and ask why they go together.

natural-wine:Amateur Bar.name: Amateur Bar
natural-wine:Amateur Bar.teaser: A Poblenou wine bar on Carrer de Llull, natural bottles by the glass and small plates for the table
natural-wine:Amateur Bar.story: Amateur sits on Carrer de Llull in Poblenou, the old factory district where warehouses became studios and the evenings now belong to small bars. It is listed on Raisin, the natural-wine app, as a dinner bar with a terrace, tastings and wine by the glass, and earlier coverage describes exposed brick, a booth of vinyl and small plates to share. The list leans to small growers and low intervention, and the staff walk you through it. It is the kind of place where one glass becomes the evening, and a good reason to stay on in Poblenou after the beach.
natural-wine:Amateur Bar.why: Sit on the terrace and ask for whatever skin-contact white they opened today.
facts: Natural wine by the glass with small plates to share

rooftops:La Caseta del Migdia.name: La Caseta del Migdia
rooftops:La Caseta del Migdia.teaser: No skyline at all: deckchairs in the pines behind Montjuïc castle, and the sea filling the view
rooftops:La Caseta del Migdia.story: La Caseta del Migdia is not on a roof. It is a clearing in the pine wood on the seaward side of Montjuïc, below the castle, with deckchairs, candles on plain tables and a DJ playing to the breeze. Look out and there is no city at all: the port's cranes, the Llobregat delta and the open sea, with the sun going down over the water in the warm months. The kitchen runs a grill, butifarra sausage and the like, and paella if you order ahead. You reach it on foot along the Mirador del Migdia path, which is half the point.
rooftops:La Caseta del Migdia.why: Walk there for sunset and stay for the music; nothing in town gives the sea this way.
facts: Mirador del Migdia, a 10–15 minute walk from Montjuïc castle (cable car up from Paral·lel)
A cold beer or vermut with the butifarra grill plate, about EUR 15 (seen Jul 2026)

rooftops:The Roof (The Barcelona EDITION.name: The Roof at the EDITION
rooftops:The Roof (The Barcelona EDITION.teaser: Ten floors over Santa Caterina's wavy roof, with Santa Maria del Mar's bell towers close enough to count
rooftops:The Roof (The Barcelona EDITION.story: The Barcelona EDITION, Ian Schrager's hotel on Avinguda de Francesc Cambó, puts its bar on the tenth floor: wood decking, a lot of green planting, a small pool, low light after dark. From the rail you look straight down onto the coloured ceramic waves of the Santa Caterina market roof and across to the Gothic towers of the cathedral and Santa Maria del Mar. Glass walls slide shut in rain and cold, so it runs all year. It takes no reservations, and the sharing plates pull a drink towards dinner.
rooftops:The Roof (The Barcelona EDITION.why: Go for the old town from above, which most rooftops here, out in the Eixample, cannot show.

rooftops:The Rooftop at Sir Victor.name: Sir Victor Rooftop
rooftops:The Rooftop at Sir Victor.teaser: A pool deck that looks straight onto the chimney warriors of La Pedrera, the Sagrada Família behind
rooftops:The Rooftop at Sir Victor.story: Sir Victor, a design hotel at Carrer del Rosselló 265, a step off Passeig de Gràcia, has a roof with a rare angle: across the street sits the back of Gaudí's Casa Milà, its helmeted chimneys at eye level, and the Sagrada Família's towers rise further off. The deck has loungers and a pool, the plates are light and made for sharing, and later in the day a DJ sets the volume. The house cocktail is the Popcorn Colada. It is a scene rather than a quiet aperitivo, and hotel guests get first claim on the loungers.
rooftops:The Rooftop at Sir Victor.why: Come in late afternoon for the Pedrera roofline in low light, before the DJ takes over.

bars:Bar Marsella.name: Bar Marsella
bars:Bar Marsella.teaser: A Raval room of marble tables and dusty bottles, reputedly open since 1820, where absinthe is still the order
bars:Bar Marsella.story: Bar Marsella on Carrer de Sant Pau is reputedly the oldest bar in Barcelona, said to have opened in 1820; no document settles the date. Nothing has been smartened: marble tables, old mirrors, bottles furred with dust, chandeliers. The Lamiel family has run it for over a century. The drink is absinthe, served with a fork, a sugar cube and a carafe of water you pour slowly until the green turns milky. In 2013, when the building was to be sold and the bar faced closure, more than 10,000 people signed a petition and the city council bought the whole building for about EUR 1.1 million to keep it.
bars:Bar Marsella.why: Do the slow pour yourself; the drink is the ritual, and there is no kitchen.
facts: Carrer de Sant Pau 65, El Raval
Absinthe with sugar cube, fork and iced water
About EUR 15 cited in one recent review (Oct 2026); cash leaning

bars:London Bar.name: London Bar
bars:London Bar.teaser: A 1910 modernista bar on Nou de la Rambla, with a trapeze hanging over the drinkers
bars:London Bar.story: Nou de la Rambla was once the street of circus and variety agents, and the London Bar opened at number 34 on 23 June 1910 to serve the performers; the 1909 on the sign is the year the premises were bought. The carved wooden back bar with its mirrors and the coloured-marble counter survive, and the bar is on the city's Ruta del Modernisme. It closed in 2017; Carlos Raluy, of the Circ Raluy circus family, inherited it and reopened it in 2018, and hung a trapeze from the ceiling. The list nods to the circus, and some nights bring flamenco or DJs.
bars:London Bar.why: Come to drink inside a 1910 room that still looks its age, not for food.
facts: Carrer Nou de la Rambla 34, El Raval, a few steps from Palau Güell

listening:Oblicuo Hi-Fi Bar.name: Oblicuo Hi-Fi Bar
listening:Oblicuo Hi-Fi Bar.teaser: A Gràcia listening bar on a hand-built sound system, vinyl only, with sake and natural wine
listening:Oblicuo Hi-Fi Bar.story: Oblicuo opened in October 2023 on Riera de Sant Miquel, taking its cue from the Japanese jazz kissa, where the record is the main event. Its founders, Ivanmaria Vele and Dobrochna Giedwidz, had the system built by the sound designer Giorgio Di Salvo, and the selectors play only vinyl: spiritual jazz one night, deep funk, Afrobeat or Brazilian records the next. Behind the bar there are cocktails, natural wine and artisan sake. The residents travel now: in April 2026 two of them, Fatal and Hanakito, played a sold-out Oblicuo night at the Triennale in Milan.

listening:Jaç Hi-Fi Café.teaser: A walnut bar that is also the speaker cabinet: specialty coffee by day, records turned up by evening
listening:Jaç Hi-Fi Café.story: Jaç opened on Avinguda Diagonal in July 2025. The name nods to jazz, and in Catalan jaç means a place to lie down and let go. Isern Serra Studio built the 95-square-metre room around one block of walnut, made by the Vidal joinery, which serves as counter, pastry display and housing for Bloom Island speakers; a walnut alcove holds the vinyl shelves. By day it serves specialty coffee, and later the music goes up, with DJ sessions on some evenings. It is not a laptop café: the cushions and the sound are there for listening.

underground:Discos Paradiso.name: Discos Paradiso
underground:Discos Paradiso.teaser: The Raval crate where the city's dance and experimental crowd crosses paths, near MACBA
underground:Discos Paradiso.story: Discos Paradiso opened in April 2010 on Carrer de Ferlandina, a few steps from MACBA, started by two diggers who had hunted records across Europe. The racks hold new and second-hand vinyl with a strong lean to electronic, leftfield and experimental music, and the shop hosts in-store sets; The Vinyl Factory put it in its series on the world's best record shops. Ten minutes away on Riera Baixa, Wah Wah Discos, open since 1992 and home of the Wah Wah Supersonic Sounds reissue label, is the other pole of Barcelona vinyl, older and rockier.

underground:Jamboree.name: Jamboree
underground:Jamboree.teaser: Spain's oldest jazz club, a vaulted cellar under Plaça Reial, open since 1960
underground:Jamboree.story: Joan Rosselló opened Jamboree in 1960 in a vaulted stone cellar under the arcades of Plaça Reial, and it claims to be the oldest jazz club in Spain. In the years when the US Sixth Fleet put into Barcelona, the touring names came down the stairs: Chet Baker, Ornette Coleman, Dexter Gordon, Stéphane Grappelli. The Mas i Mas family took it over in 1993 and still runs it. Most nights bring jazz, soul or blues sets early, then the room turns into a club after midnight. It is on every visitor's list now, and the ticket prices know it.
underground:Jamboree.why: Book the early set: the cellar at its best is a band in a stone room, not the club after.

underground:23 Robadors.teaser: A narrow Raval bar with live music every night: Wednesday jazz jam, flamenco at the weekend
underground:23 Robadors.story: 23 Robadors has run since 2004 at number 23 of Carrer d'en Robador, one of the roughest streets in the Raval, and it looks it: a narrow, scruffy room, a little stage, people pressed together. It puts on live music seven nights a week, jazz most of all, plus funk and other styles, with a jazz jam on Wednesdays and flamenco at the weekend. Working musicians come to play and to listen. In August 2026 it gave Maxi Valdés's trio a two-night stand. There are no reservations: you pay at the door and squeeze in.

underground:JazzSí Club (Taller de Músic.teaser: The Taller de Músics school's own small stage: a different style each night, a drink in the ticket
underground:JazzSí Club (Taller de Músic.story: JazzSí is the live room of the Taller de Músics, the Raval school that has trained jazz and flamenco players for decades. It is small, on Carrer de Requesens, and it programmes something nearly every night: jazz, blues, Cuban music, rock and flamenco, often with students sharing the stage with their teachers. The midweek jam belongs to the school's own players, and weekends lean flamenco. Tickets have long come with a drink included. This is the working floor of the city's music education, cheap and close-up, rather than a venue built for a crowd.

listening:Sala Apolo / Nitsa.name: Sala Apolo and Nitsa
listening:Sala Apolo / Nitsa.teaser: A 1940s Poble-sec dance hall: concerts in the evening, Nitsa's club night after midnight
listening:Sala Apolo / Nitsa.story: Sala Apolo is an old dance hall on Carrer Nou de la Rambla, near Paral·lel, the avenue of Barcelona's music halls. Its red ballroom still has the balconies and the curved bar, and it runs two lives. In the evening it is a concert room for touring and local bands. After midnight on Fridays and Saturdays it becomes Nitsa, the electronic club night that has run since the 1990s, with techno and house from local crews and visiting DJs; DJ Mag ranked it among the world's top 100 clubs. A smaller second room runs its own programme.

underground:Razzmatazz.name: Razzmatazz
underground:Razzmatazz.teaser: Five rooms under one Poblenou warehouse roof, indie in one and techno in the next
underground:Razzmatazz.story: Razzmatazz opened in 2000 in a former warehouse on Carrer dels Almogàvers in Poblenou, and it is the biggest club in the city. Five rooms run at once, The Loft, Razz Club, Lolita, Pop Bar and Rex Room, so one ticket can take you from guitar indie to hard techno across a corridor. Early in the evening the main hall is one of Barcelona's key concert stages for mid-sized touring acts; this autumn's calendar runs from Band of Horses to Tan Biónica. Expect queues, a young crowd and a long night: it rarely gets going before 01:00.
underground:Razzmatazz.why: Use the club night to move between rooms; The Loft is the one for electronic music.

underground:Moog.name: Moog
underground:Moog.teaser: A dark Raval techno room since 1996, in the old Villa Rosa flamenco tablao; thirty years old in 2026
underground:Moog.story: Moog opened on 21 June 1996 on Carrer de l'Arc del Teatre, in the rooms of the Villa Rosa flamenco tablao, and it is one of the city's longest-running electronic clubs. It is one dark room of about 400 people and a Funktion-One system: sound first, no bottle service. Jeff Mills, Laurent Garnier and Richie Hawtin have played here, but the club lives on its residents, Omar León, Uroz and Ruben Seoane among them. It marked thirty years in 2026 with a run of nights alongside Sónar in June and anniversary sets through the summer.
underground:Moog.why: Go on a weeknight when the residents play long; that is what Moog is for.
facts: Carrer de l'Arc del Teatre 3, El Raval, off the lower Rambla

listening:Rumba catalana.name: Rumba catalana
listening:Rumba catalana.teaser: Born in the gitano streets of Gràcia and the Raval: flamenco guitar played like a drum, Cuban rhythm below
listening:Rumba catalana.story: Rumba catalana is the one popular music Barcelona made for itself. It came out of the Romani (gitano) families of Gràcia, Carrer de la Cera in the Raval and Hostafrancs in the 1950s and 60s, mixing flamenco with the Cuban son and mambo heard on radio and records. Its sound is the ventilador, the fan: the guitarist's hand strikes and mutes the strings in a rolling stroke that makes the guitar a drum, credited to El Pescaílla. Peret (Pere Pubill Calaf) took it to the charts and was called its king; the Argentine-born Gato Pérez gave it a second life in the late 1970s.
listening:Rumba catalana.why: Hear it live in August at the Festes de Gràcia, in the streets where it began.
facts: Sabor de Gràcia, founded in 1994 by Antonio 'Sicus' Carbonell, keeps the Gràcia sound alive; it received the Creu de Sant Jordi in 2025 and played a free concert in Plaça de Catalunya that September. The Festes de Gràcia (15–21 August in 2026) put rumba on the street stages

Who invented it: El Pescaílla's guitar or Peret's songs, and how much was born in Barcelona rather than Madrid. Even the name is disputed: Spain's culture ministry has pushed back on 'catalana' in the long-running UNESCO bid, still undecided

underground:Heliogàbal.name: Heliogàbal
underground:Heliogàbal.teaser: An association-run Gràcia room for about 66 people, where half the city's indie scene played its first gigs
underground:Heliogàbal.story: Heliogàbal has been run by a cultural association since 1995 from a small room on Carrer de Ramón y Cajal, near Plaça Joanic. It holds about 66 people and programmes new and experimental music most nights, with poetry readings, fanzine launches and exhibitions between. It has nearly closed more than once: heavy noise-licence fines stopped its concerts in 2016, and in 2020 it warned of imminent closure. It survived, won the Ciutat de Barcelona music prize in 2012, turned thirty in 2025, and every August runs the free Festigàbal in the Jardins de la Sedeta during the Festes de Gràcia.
